claim: Demyelination in MS disrupts nerve signals and contributes to axon degeneration.
source: Demyelination in MS disrupts nerve signals and contributes to axon degeneration.
evidence: This is a general statement about MS pathology that draws from established scientific understanding of the disease.

claim: Inflammatory demyelination is accompanied by significant neuronal loss in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mouse model.
source: Inflammatory demyelination is accompanied by significant neuronal loss in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mouse model and evidence for remyelination in this model is complicated by ongoing inflammation, degeneration and possible remyelination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations in the EAE model as described in the manuscript.

claim: Oligodendroglial-specific genetic ablation of the M1 muscarinic receptor results in accelerated remyelination.
source: Oligodendroglial-specific genetic ablation of the M1 muscarinic receptor, a potent negative regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination, results in accelerated remyelination, preventing axonal loss and improving functional recovery.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from the conditional knockout mice.

claim: Accelerated remyelination prevents axonal loss in EAE.
source: Oligodendroglial-specific genetic ablation of the M1 muscarinic receptor, a potent negative regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination, results in accelerated remyelination, preventing axonal loss and improving functional recovery.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological and electron microscopy data comparing Chrm1 cKO and control mice.

claim: Accelerated remyelination improves functional recovery in EAE.
source: Oligodendroglial-specific genetic ablation of the M1 muscarinic receptor, a potent negative regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination, results in accelerated remyelination, preventing axonal loss and improving functional recovery.
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data showing reduced disease severity in Chrm1 cKO mice.

claim: Newly formed myelin remains stable at the height of inflammation due in part to the absence of MOG expression in immature myelin.
source: We demonstrate accelerated remyelination after EAE induction by direct lineage analysis and hypothesize that newly formed myelin remains stable at the height of inflammation due in part to the absence of MOG expression in immature myelin.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by lineage tracing data showing GFP-positive, MOG-negative myelin sheaths.

claim: Demyelinated axons undergo irreversible degeneration in MS, which correlates with progression and results in permanent disability.
source: Over the course of the disease, demyelinated axons undergo irreversible degeneration, which correlates with progression and results in permanent disability—events that are pathological hallmarks of progressive MS (Trapp et al., 1998; Bitsch et al., 2000; Bjartmar et al., 2003; Franklin et al., 2012; Kuhlmann et al., 2002; Lovas et al., 2000; Tallantyre et al., 2009; Trapp and Stys, 2009; Singh et al., 2013; Sorbara et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on MS pathology.

claim: There are no therapeutic interventions that directly prevent neuronal degeneration in MS.
source: To date, there are no therapeutic interventions that directly prevent neuronal degeneration, especially as the precise mechanisms underlying degeneration remain undetermined (Bjartmar and Trapp, 2003; Simons et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on the lack of neuroprotective therapies.

claim: The myelin sheath provides multiple-layers of concentric membrane, which act to maximize the speed and reduce the energy demands of action potentials.
source: As a crucial accessory to the functional nerve-fiber unit, the myelin sheath provides multiple-layers of concentric membrane, which act to maximize the speed and reduce the energy demands of action potentials.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myelin function in neuroscience.

claim: Oligodendrocytes provide critical metabolic support to neurons.
source: The importance of myelin in the developing CNS is further illustrated by recent findings demonstrating that oligodendrocytes provide critical metabolic support to neurons (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating metabolic support functions of oligodendrocytes.

claim: Remyelination is an inefficient process in MS.
source: Remyelination is an inefficient process in MS, which is likely due to an inhibitory microenvironment that prevents oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) from terminally differentiating into myelinating oligodendrocytes (Chang et al., 2002; Huang and Franklin, 2011; Kuhlmann et al., 2008; Wolswijk, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on remyelination failure in MS.

claim: The microenvironment may modify the epigenetic regulation of OPCs to alter transcriptional programs necessary for differentiation.
source: Additionally, it is thought that the microenvironment may also modify the epigenetic regulation of OPCs to alter transcriptional programs necessary for differentiation during development and after demyelination (Liu et al., 2016a, 2016b; Moyon et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on epigenetic regulation of OPCs.

claim: Recent high-throughput screening efforts have identified a number of myelin regenerative compounds.
source: In order to promote myelin repair in MS, recent high-throughput screening efforts have identified a number of myelin regenerative compounds (Deshmukh et al., 2013; Mei et al., 2014; Najm et al., 2015; Samanta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior screening studies.

claim: Some myelin regenerative compounds promote precocious differentiation of oligodendrocytes and attenuate clinical symptoms in EAE.
source: Interestingly, some of these compounds promote precocious differentiation of oligodendrocytes and attenuate clinical symptoms in EAE, an inflammatory demyelinating animal model (Liu et al., 2016b; Mei et al., 2016; Deshmukh et al., 2013; Najm et al., 2015; Samanta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies testing these compounds in EAE.

claim: Active inflammation dynamically results in coincident demyelination, axonal degeneration and remyelination in EAE.
source: The mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain unclear, as active inflammation dynamically results in coincident demyelination, axonal degeneration and remyelination (Miller and Karpus, 2007; Nikić et al., 2011; Ransohoff, 2012; Stanley and Pender, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on EAE pathology.

claim: Mice developed chronic paralysis and reached a peak clinical score approximately 14 days post immunization in MOG35-55 induced EAE.
source: The mice developed chronic paralysis and reached a peak clinical score approximately 14 days post immunization (PI), which was maintained until 30 days PI.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the EAE experiments conducted in the study.

claim: Demyelinating lesions were detected in the white matter tracts of the lumbar spinal cord at the peak of EAE severity.
source: Demyelinating lesions were detected in the white matter tracts of the lumbar spinal cord at the peak of EAE severity (Figure 1b) followed by extensive and global demyelination at the late stage of EAE (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by OsO4 staining data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Extensive and global demyelination occurs at the late stage of EAE.
source: Demyelinating lesions were detected in the white matter tracts of the lumbar spinal cord at the peak of EAE severity (Figure 1b) followed by extensive and global demyelination at the late stage of EAE (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by OsO4 staining data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Neurofilament staining displayed numerous demyelinated axons at the peak of clinical severity in EAE.
source: Notably, neurofilament (NF) staining displayed numerous demyelinated axons (MOG-negative areas) at the peak of clinical severity (Figure 1e), and significant loss of axons by NF immunoreactivity at the late stage of EAE--indicating significant neuronal degeneration (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Significant loss of axons occurs at the late stage of EAE, indicating significant neuronal degeneration.
source: Notably, neurofilament (NF) staining displayed numerous demyelinated axons (MOG-negative areas) at the peak of clinical severity (Figure 1e), and significant loss of axons by NF immunoreactivity at the late stage of EAE--indicating significant neuronal degeneration (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by NF immunostaining data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Remyelinated axons were sparsely identified as thinly myelinated axons in the late stage of EAE spinal cords by transmission electron microscopy.
source: By transmission electron microscopy (EM) (Figure 1g–i), remyelinated axons were sparsely identified as thinly myelinated axons in the late stage of EAE spinal cords, which were accompanied with a large number of demyelinated and possibly degenerating axons with diffuse cytoplasmic staining (Figure 1h,i).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figures 1g-i.

claim: The EAE model is complicated by significant inflammation, demyelination, axonal degeneration and sparse remyelination.
source: These results indicate that the EAE model is complicated by significant inflammation, demyelination, axonal degeneration and sparse remyelination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the histological and EM data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Prophylactic treatment of clemastine significantly decreased the clinical severity of EAE at the peak and throughout the chronic phase of the disease.
source: Prophylactic treatment of clemastine significantly decreased the clinical severity of EAE at the peak and throughout the chronic phase of the disease (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Clemastine treatment significantly preserved myelin staining intensity in the white matter tracts at the late stage of EAE.
source: Clemastine treatment significantly preserved myelin staining intensity and prevented axon loss as assessed by NF immunostaining in the white matter tracts at the late stage of EAE (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is supported by FluoroMyelin staining data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Clemastine treatment prevented axon loss at the late stage of EAE.
source: Clemastine treatment significantly preserved myelin staining intensity and prevented axon loss as assessed by NF immunostaining in the white matter tracts at the late stage of EAE (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is supported by NF immunostaining data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Clemastine treatment did not alter the density of CD3 or Iba1 positive cells in demyelinated lesions at the late stage of EAE.
source: We did not find a statistical difference in the density of CD3 or Iba1 positive cells after treatment with clemastine, suggesting that the mechanism of action does not alter the inflammatory response at the level of cellular infiltration (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immune cell markers shown in Figure 2e.

claim: It is impossible to conclusively determine whether clemastine contributes to the attenuation of the clinical score in EAE by solely accelerating remyelination using histology.
source: However, as histology provides a static image of one time point, it is impossible to conclusively determine whether clemastine, or any other small molecule for that matter, contributes to the attenuation of the clinical score in EAE by solely accelerating remyelination.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of histological analysis.

claim: GFP-positive myelin sheaths were visualized as 'rings' surrounding demyelinated axons after clemastine treatment at the peak of disease.
source: GFP-positive myelin was absent in the vehicle EAE mouse at the peak of disease (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), while a number of GFP positive myelin sheaths were visualized as 'rings' surrounding demyelinated axons (NF+/MOG-) after clemastine treatment (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Newly formed myelin can be initiated and identified as early as the peak of disease with myelin regenerative compounds.
source: These results directly indicate that newly formed myelin (remyelinated axons) can be initiated and identified as early as the peak of disease with myelin regenerative compounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lineage tracing data showing GFP-positive myelin at peak disease.

claim: A number of axons undergoing remyelination are surrounded by thin GFP membrane that are still yet negative for MOG expression.
source: This is clearly evident upon the detection of a number of axons surrounded by thin GFP membranes that are still yet negative for MOG expression (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The recombination efficiency of the NG2-CreErt; tau-mGFP mice is approximately 30% of the total number of oligodendrocytes.
source: By examining cortical regions where myelination is sparse at postnatal day 14, we quantified the number of GFP positive, CC1 positive oligodendrocytes and calculated a recombination efficiency of approximately 30% of the total number of oligodendrocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Clemastine may modulate the immune system via antagonism of a number of receptors expressed by immune cells.
source: Clemastine may modulate the immune system via antagonism of a number of receptors—including the histamine receptor 1 and the muscarinic receptors—expressed by immune cells (Jutel et al., 2001; Johansen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior research on clemastine's receptor targets.

claim: Clemastine and benzatropine are two potent myelin regenerative compounds that act to antagonize six overlapping targets, including the five muscarinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes and the histamine receptor 1.
source: Clemastine and benzatropine are two potent myelin regenerative compounds that act to antagonize six overlapping targets, including the five muscarinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes (Chrm1-Chrm5) and the histamine receptor 1 (Hrh1) (Cohen and Almazan, 1994; Cohen et al., 1996; De Angelis et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 1987; Ragheb et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the pharmacology of these compounds.

claim: qRT-PCR and immunostaining detected Chrm1-Chrm5 and Hrh1 expression in OPCs at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: qRT-PCR and immunostaining detected Chrm1-Chrm5 and Hrh1 expression in OPCs at both mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b) and protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clemastine or benzatropine induced an approximate five-fold increase in the number of OLs and a simultaneous decrease in the number of OPCs when examined in wildtype OPCs.
source: As expected, clemastine or benzatropine induced an approximate five-fold increase in the number of OLs and a simultaneous decrease in the number of OPCs when examined in wildtype OPCs (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from OPC cultures shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Similar effects of MR antagonists were observed in the cultures from Chrm2-Chrm5 or Hrh1 knockout OPCs.
source: Similar effects of MR antagonists were observed in the cultures from Chrm2-Chrm5 or Hrh1 knockout OPCs, suggesting that none of these individual receptors are essential for mediating the effects of the MR antagonists (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data from knockout OPC cultures shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Knockout of the Chrm1 completely abolished the effects of the anti-muscarinic compounds on OPC differentiation.
source: Interestingly, knockout of the Chrm1 completely abolished the effects of the anti-muscarinic compounds, resulting in similar numbers of OPCs and differentiated OLs as compared to vehicle-treated Chrm1KO cells, suggesting that the Chrm1 may be the sole mediator of the effects of the MR antagonists on oligodendroglia (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data from Chrm1 knockout OPC cultures shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The Chrm1 knockout cultures displayed a five-fold increase in MBP-positive OLs as well as a significant decrease in the number of OPCs when compared to wildtype cultures.
source: However, the Chrm1 knockout cultures displayed a five-fold increase in MBP-positive OLs as well as a significant decrease in the number of OPCs when compared to wildtype cultures, consistent with the hypothesis that deletion of the Chrm1 is sufficient to enhance differentiation of OPCs (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from OPC cultures shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Chrm1 null OPCs cocultured with rat DRG neurons displayed a significant increase in number of myelinating OLs as well as a concomitant decrease in OPCs.
source: To test whether OPCs from the Chrm1 knockout mice display precocious differentiation and myelination, we cocultured Chrm1 null OPCs with rat dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. We detected a significant increase in number of myelinating OLs as well as a concomitant decrease in OPCs (Figure 4d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data from DRG cocultures shown in Figures 4d and 4e.

claim: Chrm1 is a potent negative regulator of differentiation and myelination by oligodendroglia in vitro.
source: Together, our results indicate that Chrm1 is a potent negative regulator of differentiation and myelination by oligodendroglia in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro OPC culture and DRG coculture experiments.

claim: Plp in situ hybridization illustrated a significant increase in Plp-positive OLs in the lesion of Chrm1 null mice when compared to wildtype littermates at 10 dpl.
source: Plp in situ hybridization illustrated a significant increase in Plp-positive OLs in the lesion of Chrm1 null mice when compared to wildtype littermates (Figure 5b,d).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 5b and 5d.

claim: Both Mag in situ hybridization and MBP immunostaining of the lesions revealed enhanced differentiation of OLs at 10 dpl in Chrm1 knockout mice.
source: In addition, both Mag in situ hybridization (Figure 5c) and MBP immunostaining (Figure 5e) of the lesions revealed enhanced differentiation of OLs at 10 dpI in Chrm1 knockout mice.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figures 5c and 5e.

claim: Chrm1 null OPCs exhibit enhanced differentiation and accelerated kinetics of remyelination after demyelination.
source: These findings indicate that Chrm1 null OPCs exhibit enhanced differentiation and accelerated kinetics of remyelination after demyelination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lysolecithin lesion data.

claim: Chrm1 null EAE mice displayed a moderately reduced disease severity from the earliest stages of disease, followed by a remission phase with a significant decrease in clinical score from 19 days after immunization.
source: In contrast, Chrm1 null EAE mice displayed a moderately reduced disease severity from the earliest stages of disease, followed by a remission phase with a significant decrease in clinical score from 19 days after immunization (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Chrm1 knockout mice exhibited reduced areas of demyelination, suggestive of remyelination and preservation of axons when compared to wildtype EAE mice.
source: Chrm1 knockout mice exhibited reduced areas of demyelination (indicated by MOG immunoreactivity), suggestive of remyelination and preservation of axons when compared to wildtype EAE mice (Figure 5i,j).
evidence: This is supported by MOG and NF immunostaining data shown in Figures 5i and 5j.

claim: CGRP positive unmyelinated axons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord were similar in density between the naïve wildtype and Chrm1 knockout mice.
source: CGRP positive unmyelinated axons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord were similar in density between the naïve wildtype and Chrm1 knockout mice (Figure 5k,l).
evidence: This is supported by CGRP immunostaining data shown in Figures 5k and 5l.

claim: When subjected to EAE, the density of CGRP positive fibers was dramatically decreased in both Chrm1 null and wildtype mice.
source: When subjected to EAE, the density of CGRP positive fibers was dramatically decreased in both Chrm1 null and wildtype mice (Figure 5k,l).
evidence: This is supported by CGRP immunostaining data shown in Figures 5k and 5l.

claim: The decrease in the CGRP positive fibers is similar between wildtype and Chrm1 knockout mice, indicating that Chrm1 deletion does not rescue unmyelinated axons from degeneration.
source: It is noteworthy that the decrease in the CGRP positive fibers is similar between wildtype and Chrm1 knockout mice, indicating that Chrm1 deletion does not rescue unmyelinated axons from degeneration and is suggestive of the possibility that accelerated remyelination may protect axons from degeneration after EAE.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CGRP staining data comparing myelinated and unmyelinated axons.

claim: The Chrm1 cKO mice displayed similar morphologies of axons and myelin as compared to control mice by EM.
source: The Chrm1 cKO (Cnp-Cre; Chrm1 fl/fl) mice displayed similar morphologies of axons and myelin as compared to control (Chrm1 fl/fl) mice by EM.
evidence: This is supported by EM analysis of Chrm1 cKO and control mice.

claim: No significant difference was found in g-ratios between Chrm1 cKOs and controls.
source: We measured the g-ratios of myelinated axons in Chrm1 cKOs and littermate controls (Figure 6a). No significant difference was found in g-ratios between Chrm1 cKOs and controls (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by g-ratio measurements shown in Figure 6a.

claim: MOG and NF immunostaining showed comparable densities of myelinated fibers in the Chrm1 cKO and control spinal cords.
source: MOG and NF immunostaining showed comparable densities of myelinated fibers in the Chrm1 cKO and control spinal cords (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The density of differentiated oligodendrocytes was not significantly altered between Chrm1 cKOs and controls.
source: Additionally, the density of differentiated oligodendrocytes was not significantly altered between Chrm1 cKOs and controls (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by CC1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Chrm1 cKO mice display normal development of nerve fibers in adulthood.
source: These results suggest normal development of nerve fibers in adulthood of Chrm1 cKO mice (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the g-ratio, immunostaining, and oligodendrocyte density data.

claim: Disease severity of the Chrm1 cKO mice was significantly attenuated at early stages and throughout the chronic stage of EAE.
source: In contrast, disease severity of the Chrm1 cKO mice was significantly attenuated at early stages (PI 13) and throughout the chronic stage (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Chrm1 heterozygous mice revealed a moderately reduced disease severity in the early stages, followed by a remission phase and significant decrease in clinical score from 22 days after immunization.
source: Notably, Chrm1 heterozygous mice revealed a moderately reduced disease severity in the early stages, followed by a remission phase and significant decrease in clinical score from 22 days after immunization (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The cell-specific deletion of Chrm1 in OPCs is sufficient to attenuate the functional deficits elicited by EAE induction.
source: These results demonstrate that the cell-specific deletion of Chrm1 in OPCs is sufficient to attenuate the functional deficits elicited by EAE induction, and that these effects by Chrm1 inactivation may be dose-dependent as the heterozygote and homozygote mice resulted in similar clinical scores at the late stage of EAE.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clinical score data comparing Chrm1 cKO, heterozygous, and control mice.

claim: Myelinated axon density in the ventral white matter was significantly higher in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords, as compared to controls.
source: Myelinated axon density in the ventral white matter was significantly higher in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords, as compared to controls (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by toluidine blue staining data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Immunostaining for MOG and NF showed a significant increase in MOG immunoreactive areas and NF positive axons in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords, as compared to the controls.
source: Consistently, immunostaining for MOG and NF showed a significant increase in MOG immunoreactive areas and NF positive axons in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords, as compared to the controls (Figure 7d–h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 7d-h.

claim: Remyelinated axons were more consistently observed in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords compared to control EAE mice.
source: In the control EAE mice, demyelinated and degenerating axons were easily detected with a number of pre-existing myelinated axons and just a few remyelinated axons. In contrast, remyelinated axons were more consistently observed in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords (Figure 7j).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 7j.

claim: The percentage of unmyelinated axons was decreased in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords, suggesting that remyelination is enhanced in the Chrm1 cKO EAE mice.
source: The percentage of unmyelinated axons (g-ratio = 1) was decreased in the Chrm1 cKO EAE spinal cords, suggesting that remyelination is enhanced in the Chrm1 cKO EAE mice (Figure 7k).
evidence: This is supported by g-ratio analysis shown in Figure 7k.

claim: The overall myelinated axon density was significantly decreased in the EAE control mice as compared to the Chrm1 cKO mice, suggesting that less axons undergo degeneration in Chrm1 cKO EAE mice.
source: The overall myelinated axon density (per mm2) was significantly decreased in the EAE control mice as compared to the Chrm1 cKO mice, suggesting that less axons undergo degeneration in Chrm1 cKO EAE mice (Figure 7l).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of myelinated axon density shown in Figure 7l.

claim: The pre-existing myelinated axon density significantly decreased in the EAE mice, without any significant difference between the Chrm1 cKO and control EAE mice, suggesting that Chrm1 deletion in OPCs does not affect the severity of demyelination.
source: The pre-existing myelinated axon density (g-ratio < 0.8) significantly decreased in the EAE mice, without any significant difference between the Chrm1 cKO and control EAE mice, suggesting that Chrm1 deletion in OPCs does not affect the severity of demyelination (Figure 7m).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of axons with g-ratio < 0.8 shown in Figure 7m.

claim: A two-fold increase in the remyelinated axon density was detected in the Chrm1 cKO mice as compared to control EAE mice.
source: Notably, a two-fold increase in the remyelinated axon density was detected in the Chrm1 cKO mice as compared to control EAE mice (Figure 7n), demonstrating that remyelination is indeed neuroprotective from the neuroinflammatory environment in EAE.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of axons with g-ratio > 0.8 shown in Figure 7n.

claim: Remyelination is neuroprotective from the neuroinflammatory environment in EAE.
source: Notably, a two-fold increase in the remyelinated axon density was detected in the Chrm1 cKO mice as compared to control EAE mice (Figure 7n), demonstrating that remyelination is indeed neuroprotective from the neuroinflammatory environment in EAE.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased remyelinated axon density in Chrm1 cKO mice.

claim: There was no statistical difference in the number of CD3 or Iba1 positive cells in lesions from the Chrm1 cKOs and the control littermates, suggesting that the Chrm1 cKO does not overtly alter the inflammatory response.
source: We did not find a statistical difference in the number of CD3 or Iba1 positive cells in lesions from the Chrm1 cKOs and the control littermates, suggesting that the Chrm1 cKO does not overtly alter the inflammatory response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immune cell markers shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Remyelination is playing a causal role in preserving axon integrity after inflammatory demyelination.
source: While we cannot exclude the possibility that deletion of Chrm1 from OPCs may alter a yet unidentified inflammatory role by OPCs, taken together, our findings suggest that the most likely scenario is that remyelination is playing a causal role in preserving axon integrity after inflammatory demyelination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data showing accelerated remyelination, preserved axons, and no change in inflammation markers.

claim: Axonal degeneration underlies the chronic disability and progression in MS, and is currently untreatable.
source: Axonal degeneration underlies the chronic disability and progression in MS, and is currently untreatable (Bitsch et al., 2000; Bjartmar et al., 2003; Franklin et al., 2012; Kuhlmann et al., 2002; Lovas et al., 2000; Tallantyre et al., 2009; Trapp and Stys, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on MS pathology and treatment.

claim: Immunomodulatory approaches are effective in decreasing the number of relapses and may impact the timing of progressive disability but fail to fully prevent progression.
source: Immunomodulatory approaches are effective in decreasing the number of relapses and may impact the timing of progressive disability but fail to fully prevent progression (Carrithers, 2014; Rice, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on MS treatments.

claim: The myelin sheath is important to ensure the survival of axons by providing physical and metabolic support in the developing CNS.
source: Emerging evidence indicates that the myelin sheath is important to ensure the survival of axons by providing physical and metabolic support in the developing CNS (Hirrlinger and Nave, 2014; Morrison et al., 2013; Saab et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on myelin function.

claim: Remyelinating therapies have been proposed as a potential therapeutic approach for MS.
source: Since remyelination is an inefficient process in MS lesions, remyelinating therapies have been proposed as a potential therapeutic approach for MS (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on remyelination therapy.

claim: Attenuation of EAE clinical symptoms may be attributed to immunomodulatory effects from nonselective pharmacotherapeutic approaches.
source: However, our limited understanding of the significance of remyelination dampens enthusiasm for myelin regenerative approaches to protect axons and prevent progression, as attenuation of EAE clinical symptoms may also be attributed to immunomodulatory effects from nonselective pharmacotherapeutic approaches.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of interpreting pharmacological studies.

claim: For the first time, the findings uncouple remyelination from active inflammation and axonal degeneration in EAE and clearly demonstrate that remyelination is sufficient to preserve axonal integrity and neuronal function under an inflammatory demyelinating condition.
source: Here we utilize a genetic approach to enhance remyelination by manipulating oligodendroglia specifically without affecting other cell types, namely by the conditional deletion of Chrm1 in OPCs. For the first time, our findings uncouple remyelination from active inflammation and axonal degeneration in EAE and clearly demonstrate that remyelination is sufficient to preserve axonal integrity and neuronal function under an inflammatory demyelinating condition.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined experimental data from the Chrm1 cKO mice.

claim: Endogenous remyelination is nearly absent at the peak of EAE and is only sparsely observed at the later stages.
source: It is notable that endogenous remyelination is nearly absent at the peak of EAE and is only sparsely observed at the later stages, suggesting cell autonomous remyelination is an inefficient process in the inflammatory setting.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the EM and lineage tracing data showing sparse remyelination in control EAE mice.

claim: Myelin regenerative approaches are able to initiate remyelination as early as the peak of EAE.
source: Strikingly, myelin regenerative approaches are able to initiate remyelination as early as the peak of EAE, as demonstrated by lineage tracing, and is sufficient to rescue axons from degeneration, possibly by reconstructing metabolic and/or physical support for demyelinated axons.
evidence: This is supported by the lineage tracing data showing GFP-positive myelin at peak disease.

claim: Remyelinated axons are excluded from the MOG-induced demyelination due in part to the absence of MOG expression in the immature newly formed myelin.
source: Additionally, we hypothesize that remyelinated axons are excluded from the MOG-induced demyelination due in part to the absence of MOG expression in the immature newly formed myelin.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the observation of GFP-positive, MOG-negative myelin sheaths.

claim: Despite the thin myelin observed after remyelination, this process appears to be sufficient to preserve a large number of axons.
source: Furthermore despite the thin myelin observed after remyelination, this process appears to be sufficient to preserve a large number of axons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the EM data showing increased axon preservation in Chrm1 cKO mice despite thin myelin.

claim: Early remyelination could be an effective intervention to preserve axonal integrity after inflammatory demyelination.
source: This evidence suggests that early remyelination could be an effective intervention to preserve axonal integrity after inflammatory demyelination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data showing accelerated remyelination preserves axons.

claim: The findings clearly identify Chrm1 on OPCs as the target of anti-muscarinic treatment for remyelination.
source: Our findings clearly identify Chrm1 on OPCs as the target of anti-muscarinic treatment for remyelination – suggesting that remyelination therapy is a promising approach for restoring function and prolonging the quality of life for patients with MS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the receptor knockout experiments showing Chrm1 is necessary and sufficient for the effects of anti-muscarinic compounds.

claim: Remyelination therapy is a promising approach for restoring function and prolonging the quality of life for patients with MS.
source: Our findings clearly identify Chrm1 on OPCs as the target of anti-muscarinic treatment for remyelination – suggesting that remyelination therapy is a promising approach for restoring function and prolonging the quality of life for patients with MS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the clinical implications of the findings.
